sections.title: What an ecosystem is: the functional unit

board_events.text: Ecosystem = a functional unit of nature
Living organisms interact among themselves AND with their surrounding non-living environment — and keep functioning as a unit.
ABIOTIC component: light, temperature, water, soil, inorganic nutrients.
BIOTIC component — three jobs: producers (autotrophs), consumers (heterotrophs), decomposers (saprotrophs).

board_events.caption: The ecosystem as one functional unit: abiotic stock and the three biotic jobs

board_events.text: Take any one of these away and the unit stops working properly.
Producers trap sunlight and build food. Consumers eat others. Decomposers break down the dead.
Nobody is in charge — the unit runs because its parts keep interacting.

segments.text: <curious> What turns a pile of separate things into one working system? Picture your neighbourhood sabzi mandi at dawn. Vegetables arrive, money changes hands, waste piles up at the back, and a municipal cart clears it by evening.

Nobody is in charge, yet the whole thing runs as a single working unit, because its parts keep interacting. An ecosystem is exactly this: a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact among themselves and with their surrounding non-living environment, and keep functioning as a unit.
The non-living half is the abiotic component. That means light, temperature, water, soil, and the inorganic nutrients dissolved in them. These are the stage and the raw materials.

The living half is the biotic component, and it comes in exactly three jobs: producers, or autotrophs; consumers, or heterotrophs; decomposers, or saprotrophs. Notice we are naming jobs here, not creatures.

On the board: abiotic on the left, biotic on the right, arrows running both ways. Producers are the green plants, algae and photosynthetic bacteria that trap sunlight and build food. Consumers are heterotrophs that eat others. Decomposers are fungi and bacteria that break down the dead.

Underline this line. Take any one of these away and the unit stops working properly. No producers, and nothing enters the system at all. No decomposers, and everything locks up inside dead bodies forever.
So the machine reads: producers build, consumers eat, decomposers return the raw materials. Every arrow on that board is a real transfer of energy or matter, not a decoration.
And back to the mandi one last time. Nobody is in charge; the unit runs because its parts keep interacting. That single sentence is your definition, your diagram, and your first exam answer.

<curious> अलग-अलग चीज़ों का ढेर एक working system कैसे बन जाता है? सुबह की सब्ज़ी मंडी सोचिए। Vegetables आती हैं, पैसा हाथ बदलता है, पीछे waste जमा होता है, और शाम तक municipal cart उसे साफ़ कर देती है।

कोई in charge नहीं है, फिर भी पूरी मंडी एक working unit की तरह चलती है, क्योंकि उसके parts आपस में interact करते रहते हैं। Ecosystem बिलकुल यही है — nature की एक functional unit जहाँ living organisms आपस में और अपने non-living environment के साथ interact करते हैं, और एक unit की तरह चलते रहते हैं।
Non-living आधा हिस्सा है abiotic component: light, temperature, water, soil, और उनमें dissolved inorganic nutrients। यही stage है और यही raw material।

Living आधा है biotic component, और इसके ठीक तीन jobs हैं: producers यानी autotrophs, consumers यानी heterotrophs, और decomposers यानी saprotrophs। ध्यान दीजिए — हम jobs का नाम ले रहे हैं, जीवों का नहीं।

Board पर देखिए — बाएँ abiotic, दाएँ biotic, और दोनों तरफ़ arrows। Producers यानी green plants, algae और photosynthetic bacteria sunlight trap करके food बनाते हैं। Consumers दूसरों को खाते हैं। Decomposers मरे हुए को तोड़ते हैं।

यह line underline कर लीजिए। इनमें से कोई एक job हटा दीजिए और unit ठीक से चलना बंद कर देती है। Producers नहीं, तो system में कुछ अंदर आएगा ही नहीं। Decomposers नहीं, तो सब कुछ dead bodies में हमेशा के लिए lock हो जाएगा।
तो machine ऐसे पढ़िए: producers बनाते हैं, consumers खाते हैं, decomposers raw material वापस लौटाते हैं। Board का हर arrow energy या matter का असली transfer है, कोई सजावट नहीं।
और आख़िरी बार मंडी पर वापस आइए। कोई in charge नहीं है; unit चलती है क्योंकि उसके parts interact करते रहते हैं। यही एक line आपकी definition है, आपका diagram है, और आपका पहला exam answer भी।

sections.title: Scale, types, and the pond in miniature

board_events.text: How big is an ecosystem? No fixed size.
As small as the matka of water on your balcony, or a single pond. As large as a whole sal forest, or a sea.
Many ecologists treat the entire biosphere as one global ecosystem.
Two families: TERRESTRIAL — forest, grassland, desert. AQUATIC — pond, lake, wetland, river, estuary.
The pond is the classic teaching example: small, self-sustaining, and yet it contains every structural and functional piece in miniature.

board_events.text: Pond abiotic: the water itself, with all inorganic and organic substances dissolved in it, plus the light and warmth reaching it.
Pond producers: floating phytoplankton, algae, and the submerged and marginal plants. Consumers: zooplankton and fish. Decomposers: fungi, bacteria, flagellates at the bottom.
Self-sustaining = nothing is imported daily. The same fixed energy and recycled nutrients keep the unit ticking.

segments.text: How big is an ecosystem? There is no fixed size, and that is the point. It can be as small as the matka of water sitting on your balcony, or a single pond.
And it can be as large as a whole sal forest, or a sea. Many ecologists go one step further and treat the entire biosphere as one global ecosystem.
That range would be unmanageable to study, so we split ecosystems into two families. Terrestrial: forest, grassland, desert. Aquatic: pond, lake, wetland, river, estuary.
The pond is the classic teaching example, and for a good reason. It is small, it is self-sustaining, and yet it contains every structural and functional piece in miniature.
So look closely at the pond on the board. The whole machine is running in one shallow water body, and you can see all of it at once.
Its abiotic part is the water itself, with all the inorganic and organic substances dissolved in it, plus the light and the warmth reaching it from above.
Its producers are the floating phytoplankton, the algae, and the submerged and marginal plants that trap the sun's energy.
Its consumers are the zooplankton and the fish that feed along the chain. And its decomposers — fungi, bacteria and flagellates — work mainly at the bottom, where the dead settle.

Here is what self-sustaining actually means: none of this is imported from outside on a daily basis. The same fixed energy and the same recycled nutrients keep the unit ticking. Read the pond this way, and every later idea in this chapter already has a home.
Ecosystem कितना बड़ा होता है? कोई fixed size नहीं है, और यही तो बात है। यह उतना छोटा हो सकता है जितना आपकी balcony पर रखा पानी का matka, या एक अकेला pond।
और उतना बड़ा भी, जितना पूरा sal forest, या एक समुद्र। कई ecologists एक कदम आगे जाकर पूरे biosphere को ही एक global ecosystem मानते हैं।
इतनी range पढ़ना मुश्किल हो जाता, इसलिए हम ecosystems को दो families में बाँटते हैं। Terrestrial: forest, grassland, desert. Aquatic: pond, lake, wetland, river, estuary.
Pond classic teaching example है, और वजह अच्छी है। यह छोटा है, self-sustaining है, और फिर भी हर structural और functional piece इसमें miniature में मौजूद है।
तो board पर pond को ध्यान से देखिए। पूरी machine एक उथले water body में चल रही है, और आप उसे एक ही नज़र में देख सकते हैं।
इसका abiotic हिस्सा है पानी ख़ुद, उसमें dissolved सारे inorganic और organic substances, और ऊपर से आती हुई light और warmth।
इसके producers हैं floating phytoplankton, algae, और submerged तथा marginal plants, जो सूरज की energy trap करते हैं।
इसके consumers हैं zooplankton और मछलियाँ, जो chain के साथ खाती हैं। और decomposers — fungi, bacteria और flagellates — ज़्यादातर तल पर काम करते हैं, जहाँ मरे हुए जीव बैठते हैं।

Self-sustaining का असली मतलब यह है: इनमें से कुछ भी रोज़ बाहर से import नहीं होता। वही fixed energy और वही recycled nutrients unit को चलाते रहते हैं। Pond को इस तरह पढ़िए, और chapter का हर आगे वाला idea अपने आप जगह पा लेगा।

sections.title: Structure: species composition and stratification

board_events.text: STRUCTURE = the two S's
Species composition — which plant and animal species live here. Found by identification and enumeration.
Stratification — the vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels.

board_events.text: In a forest: tall trees take the top stratum, shrubs the middle, herbs and grasses the bottom.
Stratification is MORE pronounced in a tropical rainforest than in a temperate forest — the vertical structure there is far more complex.
Both are STRUCTURAL. Never functional. Examiners plant 'stratification is a functional unit' as a false statement.
School analogy: the attendance register is species composition. The floor each class sits on is stratification.

segments.text: An ecosystem has two structural faces, and they are easy to hold together if you call them the two S's: species composition, and stratification.
Species composition is the guest-list. Which plant and animal species actually live here? You answer it by identification and enumeration — naming them, and counting them. Nothing more, nothing less.
Stratification is the seating plan. It is the vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels of the same place.
Look at the board. On the left, a list of names. On the right, the same forest cut into horizontal bands. Same forest — two completely different questions asked about it.
In a forest, the tall trees occupy the top stratum and take first claim on the light. Shrubs occupy the middle. Herbs and grasses sit at the bottom, in the shade.
Now a comparison worth remembering. Stratification is more pronounced in a tropical rainforest than in a temperate forest, because the vertical structure there is far more complex.

And here is the exam-critical line. Both of these are structural features. Never functional. Examiners love planting the statement that stratification is a functional unit — it is false, every single time it appears.

Treat the ecosystem like your school. The attendance register — who is enrolled — is its species composition. The floor each class sits on, seniors upstairs and juniors below, is its stratification. Register and floor plan together describe the structure; the actual teaching, exams and canteen sales are the function.
Ecosystem के दो structural चेहरे होते हैं, और इन्हें याद रखना आसान है अगर आप इन्हें दो S कह दें: species composition और stratification.
Species composition guest-list है। यहाँ कौन-कौन से plant और animal species रहते हैं? इसका जवाब identification और enumeration से मिलता है — नाम गिनाना और गिनती करना। इससे ज़्यादा कुछ नहीं।
Stratification seating plan है। यह अलग-अलग species का vertical distribution है, जो एक ही जगह के अलग-अलग levels पर रहते हैं।
Board देखिए। बाईं तरफ़ नामों की list। दाईं तरफ़ वही forest, horizontal bands में कटा हुआ। एक ही forest — पर दो बिलकुल अलग सवाल।
Forest में tall trees top stratum लेते हैं और light पर पहला हक़ जमाते हैं। Shrubs बीच में रहते हैं। Herbs और grasses सबसे नीचे, छाँव में।
अब एक comparison जो याद रखने लायक़ है। Stratification tropical rainforest में temperate forest के मुक़ाबले ज़्यादा pronounced होता है, क्योंकि वहाँ vertical structure कहीं ज़्यादा complex है।
और यह रही exam-critical line। ये दोनों structural features हैं। Functional कभी नहीं। Examiners यह statement बड़े शौक़ से डालते हैं कि stratification एक functional unit है — यह हर बार ग़लत होता है।

Ecosystem को अपना school मान लीजिए। Attendance register — कौन enrolled है — यह है species composition। हर class किस floor पर बैठती है, seniors ऊपर juniors नीचे — यह है stratification। Register और floor plan मिलकर structure बताते हैं; असली पढ़ाई, exams और canteen की बिक्री function है।

sections.title: Productivity: a rate, never a stock

board_events.text: Productivity — the first FUNCTIONAL aspect
Think of the ecosystem as a business. The producers are the only earners — they earn energy by photosynthesis.
Some of that income is spent immediately on the producers' own running costs: respiration.
Whatever is left over is the savings that everyone higher up — herbivores, carnivores, decomposers — gets to live on.

board_events.text: Productivity = the rate at which biomass is built, per unit area per unit time. A flow, like monthly income — never a one-time lump.
The commonest slip: confusing the rate with the biomass standing there at a moment. That stock is called STANDING CROP.
Limit 1: ecosystem boundaries are a convenience. Real ecosystems are open — a pond and its catchment are not truly sealed.
Limit 2: an ecosystem can be incomplete. An aquarium, or the deep aphotic ocean, lacks producers — so it cannot self-sustain.

segments.text: Structure told us who is here and how they are stacked. Now the first functional aspect: productivity. And the cleanest way in is to treat the ecosystem as a business.

In this business, the producers are the only earners. They earn energy by photosynthesis. Nobody else brings income into the system — every unit of energy that ever circulates here was earned by a green plant.
Some of that income is spent immediately, on the producers' own running costs. That cost is respiration — the energy a plant burns simply to stay alive.
Whatever is left over is the savings, and that is what everyone higher up lives on: herbivores, carnivores, decomposers, all of them, without exception.
<excited> Now look hard at this board, because this one comparison is where marks quietly disappear. On the left, a flow. On the right, a tank.
Productivity is the rate at which this biomass is built, per unit area per unit time. It is a flow, like monthly income — never a one-time lump.

The single most common conceptual slip in this chapter is confusing that rate with the amount of biomass standing there at a moment. That stock has its own name — standing crop — and the two are not interchangeable.

Two honest limits before we move on. Ecosystem boundaries are a convenience. Real ecosystems are open — they exchange energy and matter with their neighbours. A pond and its catchment are not truly sealed.
And an ecosystem can be incomplete. An aquarium, or the deep aphotic ocean, lacks producers. So it cannot self-sustain, and it depends on outside input to keep going at all.
Structure ने बताया कि यहाँ कौन है और वे कैसे stacked हैं। अब पहला functional aspect: productivity। और इसे समझने का सबसे साफ़ रास्ता है — ecosystem को एक business मान लेना।
इस business में producers ही अकेले earners हैं। वे photosynthesis से energy कमाते हैं। कोई और system में income नहीं लाता — यहाँ जो भी energy घूमती है, वह किसी green plant ने ही कमाई है।
उस income का कुछ हिस्सा तुरंत ख़र्च हो जाता है, producers के अपने running costs पर। वह cost है respiration — वह energy जो पौधा सिर्फ़ ज़िंदा रहने के लिए जलाता है।
जो बचता है वह savings है, और उसी पर ऊपर वाले सब जीते हैं: herbivores, carnivores, decomposers — सब के सब।
<excited> अब इस board को ध्यान से देखिए, क्योंकि यही एक comparison है जहाँ चुपचाप marks उड़ जाते हैं। बाईं तरफ़ एक flow। दाईं तरफ़ एक tank।
Productivity वह rate है जिस पर biomass बनती है — per unit area, per unit time। यह एक flow है, monthly income की तरह — कभी one-time lump नहीं।
इस chapter की सबसे आम conceptual ग़लती यही है: इस rate को उस biomass से confuse कर देना जो किसी एक पल में वहाँ खड़ी है। उस stock का अपना नाम है — standing crop — और दोनों interchangeable नहीं हैं।

आगे बढ़ने से पहले दो ईमानदार limits। Ecosystem की boundaries हमारी सहूलियत हैं। असली ecosystems open होते हैं — वे पड़ोसियों के साथ energy और matter exchange करते हैं। Pond और उसका catchment सचमुच sealed नहीं हैं।
और ecosystem incomplete भी हो सकता है। Aquarium, या गहरा aphotic ocean — इनमें producers नहीं होते। इसलिए वे self-sustain नहीं कर सकते, और चलते रहने के लिए बाहर के input पर निर्भर रहते हैं।

sections.title: Framework A: how to describe any ecosystem

board_events.text: FRAMEWORK A — describing any ecosystem's structure
Step 1: list the abiotic stock — light, temperature, water, soil, inorganic nutrients.
Step 2: sort the biotic members into the three functional jobs — producers, consumers, decomposers.
Why this order? Energy and matter enter ONLY through producers, so they anchor the description.

board_events.text: Step 3: record species composition (who is present) and stratification (how they are layered). Both structural.
Step 4: classify as terrestrial or aquatic. Then check completeness — are producers present?
No producers (aquarium, deep sea) = an incomplete, non-self-sustaining ecosystem.

segments.text: Ecology has no algebraic derivation to offer here, so the work is procedural. What you are learning is how to read and account for an ecosystem, not how to derive a formula. Here is the routine.
Step one: list the abiotic stock. Light, temperature, water, soil, and inorganic nutrients. Get the non-living inventory down first, because everything else is built on it.
Step two: sort the biotic members into the three functional jobs — producers, consumers, decomposers. Do not sort them by size or by how familiar they are. Sort them by what they do.

And why in that order? Because energy and matter enter the system only through producers. They are the doorway, so they anchor the whole description. Start anywhere else and your account has no beginning.
The board lays the routine out as four gates. Notice that each one asks a different question, and you never skip ahead.
Step three: record species composition — who is present — and stratification — how they are layered. Both of these are structural features. Both. Never functional.
Step four: classify the ecosystem as terrestrial or aquatic, and then run the completeness check. Ask one question: are producers present?
If the answer is no — as in an aquarium, or in the deep aphotic ocean — then it is an incomplete, non-self-sustaining ecosystem, and something must be supplied from outside for it to persist at all.
यहाँ ecology के पास कोई algebraic derivation नहीं है, इसलिए काम procedural है। आप यह सीख रहे हैं कि ecosystem को कैसे पढ़ें और उसका हिसाब कैसे लगाएँ, कोई formula derive करना नहीं। तो यह रही routine।
Step एक: abiotic stock की list बनाइए। Light, temperature, water, soil, और inorganic nutrients. पहले non-living inventory उतार लीजिए, क्योंकि बाक़ी सब कुछ उसी पर खड़ा है।
Step दो: biotic members को तीन functional jobs में छाँटिए — producers, consumers, decomposers। इन्हें size से या जान-पहचान से मत छाँटिए। इन्हें इस आधार पर छाँटिए कि वे करते क्या हैं।

और इसी order में क्यों? क्योंकि energy और matter system में सिर्फ़ producers के रास्ते ही घुसते हैं। वही दरवाज़ा हैं, इसलिए वही पूरे description को anchor करते हैं। कहीं और से शुरू कीजिए, और आपके account की कोई शुरुआत ही नहीं होगी।
Board इस routine को चार gates की तरह रखता है। ध्यान दीजिए कि हर gate एक अलग सवाल पूछता है, और आप कभी आगे नहीं कूदते।
Step तीन: species composition record कीजिए — कौन मौजूद है — और stratification — वे कैसे layered हैं। ये दोनों structural features हैं। दोनों। Functional कभी नहीं।
Step चार: ecosystem को terrestrial या aquatic classify कीजिए, और फिर completeness check चलाइए। सिर्फ़ एक सवाल पूछिए: क्या producers मौजूद हैं?
अगर जवाब नहीं है — जैसे aquarium में, या गहरे aphotic ocean में — तो वह एक incomplete, non-self-sustaining ecosystem है, और उसे टिके रहने के लिए बाहर से कुछ न कुछ देना ही पड़ेगा।

sections.title: The productivity account: GPP, R and NPP

board_events.text: The producers' income statement
Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) — the total rate of organic-matter production by producers through photosynthesis, INCLUDING what is later used up in respiration.
R = respiratory loss by the PRODUCERS. Not by decomposers. A classic trap.
Net Primary Productivity (NPP) — the organic matter left with producers after their own respiratory loss. This is the biomass actually available to heterotrophs.

board_events.caption: GPP as gross income, R as running cost, NPP as savings, and secondary productivity above it

board_events.text: Secondary productivity — the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers. Smaller, and it shrinks further up each trophic level.
Units of productivity — mass form: grams per square metre per year. Energy form: kilocalories per square metre per year.
Note the unit's structure: mass or energy, divided by area, divided by time. The two divisions are what make it a RATE.

segments.text: Treat this as an income statement for the producers, and every term lands in the right place. There are only three numbers on the sheet, and one relation between them.

Start with gross primary productivity. G P P is the total rate of organic-matter production by producers through photosynthesis — and critically, it includes what is later used up in respiration. It is gross income, before any deduction.
Here is the relation, and it is the single most examined line in this subtopic. N P P equals G P P minus R.
Now the trap, and it is a famous one. R is the respiratory loss by the producers. By the producers. Not by decomposers, not by consumers. Decomposers do not enter this equation at all.
So net primary productivity is the organic matter left with the producers after their own respiratory loss has been met. And that leftover is precisely the biomass actually available to heterotrophs.

The board shows the split. Gross income comes in, the running cost peels off downward, and what carries forward is the savings. Why subtract? Because you cannot bank energy you have already burned to stay alive.

One more term to place. At the consumer level, the rate of formation of new organic matter is called secondary productivity. It is smaller than primary productivity, and it shrinks further at every step up — because each level only ever receives the leftover, and spends its own respiration before passing anything on.
Units now. Productivity comes in two forms. Mass form: grams per square metre per year. Energy form: kilocalories per square metre per year. Biology uses units, not dimensional formulae.

And read the structure of that unit, because it is the whole idea in miniature. Mass or energy, divided by area, divided by time. Those two divisions are exactly what make it a rate per area — and not a lump sitting somewhere.
इसे producers का income statement मान लीजिए, और हर term अपनी सही जगह बैठ जाएगा। Sheet पर सिर्फ़ तीन numbers हैं, और उनके बीच एक relation।

शुरुआत gross primary productivity से। G P P producers द्वारा photosynthesis से organic matter बनाने का total rate है — और ज़रूरी बात, इसमें वह भी शामिल है जो बाद में respiration में ख़र्च हो जाता है। यह gross income है, किसी deduction से पहले।
यह रहा relation, और यही इस subtopic की सबसे ज़्यादा पूछी जाने वाली line है। N P P बराबर G P P minus R.
अब trap, और यह मशहूर है। R है producers का respiratory loss। Producers का। Decomposers का नहीं, consumers का नहीं। Decomposers इस equation में आते ही नहीं।
तो net primary productivity वह organic matter है जो producers के पास उनका अपना respiratory loss पूरा होने के बाद बचता है। और वही बचा हुआ हिस्सा heterotrophs के लिए असल में available biomass है।

Board split दिखा रहा है। Gross income अंदर आती है, running cost नीचे की तरफ़ निकल जाती है, और जो आगे बढ़ता है वह savings है। घटाते क्यों हैं? क्योंकि जो energy आप ज़िंदा रहने के लिए पहले ही जला चुके हैं, उसे bank नहीं कर सकते।

एक और term जगह पर रख लीजिए। Consumer level पर नया organic matter बनने का rate secondary productivity कहलाता है। यह primary से छोटा होता है, और हर ऊपर वाले step पर और सिकुड़ता है — क्योंकि हर level को सिर्फ़ बचा हुआ ही मिलता है, और वह भी अपना respiration पहले ख़र्च करता है।
अब units। Productivity दो रूपों में आती है। Mass form: grams per square metre per year। Energy form: kilocalories per square metre per year। Biology में units चलती हैं, dimensional formulae नहीं।
और उस unit की बनावट पढ़िए, क्योंकि पूरा idea उसी में छिपा है। Mass या energy, area से भाग, फिर time से भाग। यही दो भाग इसे rate per area बनाते हैं — कहीं पड़ा हुआ lump नहीं।

sections.title: Stock terms, and how productivity is measured

board_events.text: Stocks, and the measurement of a rate
Standing crop — the amount of living biomass present at a trophic level at a given time. Measured as DRY weight (water content varies and would distort fresh-weight comparisons).
Standing state — the amount of nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon) present in the soil at a given time. It differs between ecosystems and between seasons.

board_events.text: Biomass — the total dry mass of all organisms in the ecosystem: producers + consumers + decomposers + dead matter.
Factors governing primary productivity: availability of nutrients, and the photosynthetic capacity of the plants.
Together with environmental factors: temperature, water and precipitation, light, and incident solar radiation.

segments.text: Before the numericals, lock down the two stock terms — because the exam separates them by exactly one word, and rewards you a full mark for knowing which.

Standing crop is the amount of living biomass present at a trophic level at a given time. And it is always measured as dry weight, because water content varies from sample to sample and would distort any fresh-weight comparison.

Standing state is a different animal entirely. It is the amount of nutrients — nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon — present in the soil at a given time. It differs between ecosystems, and it differs between seasons in the same ecosystem.

Now, how is productivity actually measured? It shows up as an increase in dry mass, and there are two standard ways to report that gain. First, relative growth rate. R G R is the increase in dry mass in unit time, divided by the dry mass of the plant.

Second, net assimilation rate. N A R is the increase in dry mass in unit time, divided by the leaf area. Same numerator, different denominator — and the denominator is what each measure is really about.

The board makes the difference obvious. R G R gives you gain per existing gram, so a seedling and a full-grown tree can be compared fairly. N A R gives you gain per photosynthesising surface — how good the factory floor is, not how big the factory is.
One more term. Biomass is the total dry mass of all organisms in the ecosystem: producers, plus consumers, plus decomposers, plus dead matter. Everything, weighed dry.

Which brings the obvious question — why dry mass throughout? Because fresh weight swings with water content. Dry weight gives a fair, repeatable measure. It is the same reason standing crop is reported as dry weight.

Finally, what governs primary productivity in the first place. Two things by name: availability of nutrients, and the photosynthetic capacity of the plants. Together with environmental factors — temperature, water and precipitation, light, and incident solar radiation.
Numericals से पहले दोनों stock terms पक्के कर लीजिए — क्योंकि exam इन्हें ठीक एक शब्द से अलग करता है, और सही पहचानने पर पूरा एक mark देता है।

Standing crop वह living biomass है जो किसी trophic level पर किसी दिए हुए समय पर मौजूद है। और इसे हमेशा dry weight में नापा जाता है, क्योंकि पानी की मात्रा sample दर sample बदलती है और fresh-weight comparison को बिगाड़ देती।

Standing state बिलकुल अलग चीज़ है। यह मिट्टी में किसी समय पर मौजूद nutrients की मात्रा है — nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon। यह अलग-अलग ecosystems में अलग होती है, और एक ही ecosystem में मौसम के साथ भी बदलती है।

अब, productivity नापी कैसे जाती है? यह dry mass में बढ़ोतरी के रूप में दिखती है, और उस gain को बताने के दो standard तरीक़े हैं। पहला, relative growth rate। R G R है unit time में dry mass की बढ़ोतरी, भाग पौधे का dry mass।
दूसरा, net assimilation rate। N A R है unit time में dry mass की बढ़ोतरी, भाग leaf area। Numerator वही, denominator अलग — और denominator ही बताता है कि माप असल में किस बारे में है।

Board फ़र्क़ साफ़ कर देता है। R G R देता है हर मौजूद gram पर gain, तो एक seedling और एक पूरा पेड़ ठीक से compare हो सकते हैं। N A R देता है हर photosynthesising surface पर gain — factory का floor कितना अच्छा है, factory कितनी बड़ी है यह नहीं।
एक और term। Biomass है ecosystem के सारे organisms का total dry mass: producers, plus consumers, plus decomposers, plus dead matter। सब कुछ, सूखा तौला हुआ।

अब साफ़ सवाल — हर जगह dry mass ही क्यों? क्योंकि fresh weight पानी के साथ ऊपर-नीचे होता रहता है। Dry weight एक fair और repeatable माप देता है। यही वजह है कि standing crop भी dry weight में ही बताया जाता है।

आख़िर में, primary productivity को चलाता क्या है। दो चीज़ें नाम से: nutrients की availability, और पौधों की photosynthetic capacity। इनके साथ environmental factors — temperature, water और precipitation, light, और incident solar radiation।

board_events.text: Answer: NPP = 16,000 kcal per square metre per year — the energy available to the herbivores and decomposers of this grassland.
Marks are routinely lost for dropping the units or the 'per year'. Carry the full rate-unit to the final line.
Example 2 — CUET / Speed Trap
A farmer says: 'I harvested 12 quintals of wheat in 0.5 hectare, 150 days after sowing.' A student labels this the field's GPP. Correct?
It gives amount, area AND time — so it CAN be expressed as a productivity. But it is NET, not gross: the harvested grain is what the crop kept after its own respiration.
Elimination cue: 'what's left / what we collect' means net. 'Total photosynthesis' means gross.

segments.text: Example one, from the C B S E boards. A grassland plot. Its gross primary productivity is measured as twenty five thousand kilocalories per square metre per year, and the respiratory loss by the producers is nine thousand kilocalories per square metre per year. Calculate the net primary productivity, with units.

Write down what you are given before you do anything else. G P P is twenty five thousand. R is nine thousand. Both in kilocalories per square metre per year — and the moment the units match, the subtraction is legal.
The picture on the board is the entire answer in one glance. The tall green bar is the gross income. The red bar is what the producers burn just to stay alive. What survives is the blue bar.
The relation you need is the only one there is. N P P equals G P P minus R. Nothing else enters — no decomposers, no consumers. This is the producers' own account.

Substitute and finish. Twenty five thousand minus nine thousand gives sixteen thousand kilocalories per square metre per year. And say what it means: that is the energy available to the herbivores and the decomposers of this grassland.
<whisper> Here is where marks quietly disappear. Students reach sixteen thousand and then write it bare, or drop the per year. Carry the full rate-unit all the way to the final line. Every time.

Example two, a C U E T speed trap. A farmer says: I harvested twelve quintals of wheat in half a hectare, one hundred and fifty days after sowing. A student labels this the field's G P P. Is that correct? Answer fast.

Check the shape of the claim first. A productivity is a rate per area per time. The statement does give an amount, an area, and a time — so it genuinely could be expressed as a productivity. That half of the student's thinking is fine.

But it would be net, not gross. The harvested grain is matter the crop kept after its own respiration. That is net primary productivity. Gross would additionally include everything the plant had already respired away — and nobody ever harvests that.

So the answer: it is incorrect to call it G P P. As a per-area-per-time figure it represents net primary productivity. And bank the elimination cue — anything worded as what's left, or what we collect, means net. Total photosynthesis means gross.

Example एक, C B S E boards से। एक grassland plot। इसकी gross primary productivity नापी गई है पच्चीस हज़ार kilocalories per square metre per year, और producers का respiratory loss है नौ हज़ार kilocalories per square metre per year। Net primary productivity निकालिए, units के साथ।
कुछ भी करने से पहले given लिख लीजिए। G P P है पच्चीस हज़ार। R है नौ हज़ार। दोनों kilocalories per square metre per year में — और जैसे ही units मिल जाती हैं, subtraction जायज़ हो जाता है।
Board की तस्वीर पूरा जवाब एक नज़र में दे देती है। ऊँचा हरा bar gross income है। लाल bar वह है जो producers सिर्फ़ ज़िंदा रहने के लिए जलाते हैं। जो बचता है वह नीला bar है।
आपको जो relation चाहिए, बस वही एक है। N P P बराबर G P P minus R। और कुछ नहीं घुसता — न decomposers, न consumers। यह producers का अपना account है।

Substitute कीजिए और ख़त्म कीजिए। पच्चीस हज़ार minus नौ हज़ार बराबर सोलह हज़ार kilocalories per square metre per year। और मतलब भी लिखिए: यही energy है जो इस grassland के herbivores और decomposers को मिलेगी।
<whisper> यहीं marks चुपचाप ग़ायब होते हैं। Students सोलह हज़ार तक पहुँचकर उसे ऐसे ही लिख देते हैं, या per year गिरा देते हैं। पूरी rate-unit आख़िरी line तक साथ ले जाइए। हर बार।

Example दो, एक C U E T speed trap। एक किसान कहता है: मैंने आधे hectare में बारह quintal गेहूँ काटा, बुवाई के एक सौ पचास दिन बाद। एक student इसे field की G P P कह देता है। क्या यह सही है? जल्दी जवाब दीजिए।

पहले claim की शक्ल जाँचिए। Productivity एक rate है — per area, per time। Statement में amount है, area है, और time भी है — तो इसे सचमुच productivity की तरह express किया जा सकता है। सोच का यह आधा हिस्सा ठीक है।

पर यह net होगी, gross नहीं। काटा हुआ अनाज वह matter है जो फ़सल ने अपना respiration पूरा करने के बाद रखा। यानी net primary productivity। Gross में वह सब भी जुड़ता जो पौधा पहले ही respire कर चुका — और उसे कोई नहीं काटता।

तो जवाब: इसे G P P कहना ग़लत है। Per-area-per-time figure के तौर पर यह net primary productivity है। और elimination cue याद रखिए — जो बचा, या जो हमने इकट्ठा किया, ऐसा wording मतलब net। Total photosynthesis मतलब gross।

board_events.text: Step 1 — placement: the four FUNCTIONAL aspects are productivity, decomposition, energy flow, nutrient cycling. Species composition and stratification are structural. So productivity is FUNCTIONAL.
Step 2 — field: sugarcane is a highly efficient photosynthesiser, with abundant nutrients and water from cultivation. Photosynthetic capacity + nutrient availability dominate.
Step 3 — pond: light penetration falls sharply with depth, so producers below the surface are starved of light. The dominant limiting factor is light availability with depth.
Example 4 — NEET / Assertion-Reason
A: The NPP of an ecosystem can never exceed its GPP. R: NPP is the biomass available to heterotrophs after the producers' respiratory losses are met.
A is true: since NPP = GPP - R and R is never negative, NPP is at most equal to GPP. R is true, and it states exactly WHY GPP is reduced to NPP. So R IS the correct explanation. Answer: (i).
Trap: candidates who misremember the relation as NPP = GPP + R wrongly mark A false and pick (iv).

segments.text: Example three, from N E E T. A shallow village pond and a nearby sugarcane field receive similar sunlight. Yet the field shows much higher primary productivity. Two factors are at play — identify the dominant one in each system, and state which functional aspect productivity belongs to.

Do not jump to the biology. First place the term, because the question asks you to. Productivity is one of the four functional aspects of an ecosystem: productivity, decomposition, energy flow, nutrient cycling. Stratification and species composition are the structural ones. So productivity is functional.
Now look at the two panels on the board side by side. Same sun overhead in both. Everything that differs is happening below that sun.

Take the field. Sugarcane is a highly efficient photosynthesiser, and cultivation hands it abundant nutrients and water. So here the photosynthetic capacity of the plant and nutrient availability are what dominate. Nothing is holding it back.

Now the pond. In water bodies, light penetration falls sharply with depth. Producers below the surface are simply starved of light — they have the nutrients, they have the water, but the energy never reaches them. The dominant limiting factor is light availability with depth.

So the full answer reads: field, high productivity from photosynthetic capacity and nutrient supply; pond, limited by light penetration; and productivity is a functional aspect. All three parts, or you lose the mark.

Example four, a high-difficulty N E E T assertion-reason. Assertion: the net primary productivity of an ecosystem can never exceed its gross primary productivity. Reason: net primary productivity is the biomass available to heterotrophs after the producers' respiratory losses are met.

Evaluate the assertion first, always. Since N P P equals G P P minus R, and respiration is never negative, N P P is at most equal to G P P — and equal only if R were zero, which never holds for living producers. So the assertion is true.
Now evaluate the reason on its own. N P P is indeed G P P minus the producers' respiration, and it is precisely the biomass passed on to heterotrophs. So the reason is true as well.

The last question is the one that decides the option. Does the reason explain the assertion? Yes — it states why G P P is reduced to N P P, and subtracting a non-negative respiration term is exactly the reason N P P cannot exceed G P P. So the answer is option one. And the trap: anyone who misremembers the relation as G P P plus R marks the assertion false and picks option four.

Example तीन, N E E T से। एक उथला गाँव का pond और पास का एक sugarcane field — दोनों को लगभग बराबर sunlight मिलती है। फिर भी field की primary productivity कहीं ज़्यादा है। दो factors काम कर रहे हैं — हर system में dominant वाला पहचानिए, और बताइए कि productivity कौन-सा functional aspect है।

Biology पर मत कूदिए। पहले term को जगह दीजिए, क्योंकि सवाल यही माँग रहा है। Productivity ecosystem के चार functional aspects में से एक है: productivity, decomposition, energy flow, nutrient cycling। Stratification और species composition structural हैं। तो productivity functional है।
अब board के दोनों panels साथ-साथ देखिए। दोनों के ऊपर वही सूरज। जो भी फ़र्क़ है, वह उस सूरज के नीचे हो रहा है।

पहले field। Sugarcane बहुत efficient photosynthesiser है, और खेती उसे भरपूर nutrients और पानी देती है। तो यहाँ पौधे की photosynthetic capacity और nutrient availability ही dominate करती हैं। कुछ भी उसे रोक नहीं रहा।

अब pond। पानी में light penetration गहराई के साथ तेज़ी से गिरती है। सतह के नीचे वाले producers बस light के लिए तरस जाते हैं — nutrients हैं, पानी है, पर energy उन तक पहुँचती ही नहीं। Dominant limiting factor है गहराई के साथ light availability।

तो पूरा जवाब ऐसे बनता है: field में photosynthetic capacity और nutrient supply से high productivity; pond में light penetration की limit; और productivity एक functional aspect है। तीनों हिस्से लिखिए, वरना mark गया।

Example चार, high-difficulty N E E T assertion-reason। Assertion: किसी ecosystem की net primary productivity उसकी gross primary productivity से कभी ज़्यादा नहीं हो सकती। Reason: net primary productivity वह biomass है जो producers का respiratory loss पूरा होने के बाद heterotrophs को मिलती है।

हमेशा पहले assertion जाँचिए। चूँकि N P P बराबर G P P minus R, और respiration कभी negative नहीं होता, इसलिए N P P ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा G P P के बराबर हो सकती है — और बराबर तभी, जब R शून्य हो, जो ज़िंदा producers में कभी नहीं होता। तो assertion सही है।
अब reason को अलग से जाँचिए। N P P सचमुच G P P minus producers का respiration है, और वही biomass heterotrophs तक जाती है। तो reason भी सही है।

आख़िरी सवाल ही option तय करता है। क्या reason, assertion को explain करता है? हाँ — वह बताता है कि G P P घटकर N P P क्यों होती है, और एक non-negative respiration term घटाना ही वह वजह है कि N P P, G P P से ऊपर नहीं जा सकती। तो जवाब है option एक। और trap: जो relation को G P P plus R याद रखते हैं, वे assertion को ग़लत मानकर option चार चुन बैठते हैं।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips: rate vs stock, and the respiration trap

board_events.text: Four traps that decide your marks here
1. Productivity (rate) vs standing crop (stock). Watch the wording: 'rate of...' means productivity; 'amount at a time' means standing crop.
2. The respiration trap: NPP = GPP - R of PRODUCERS. NOT GPP minus decomposition. And definitely not GPP + R. Decomposers do not enter this equation.
3. Structure vs function mix-up. Species composition and stratification are STRUCTURAL. Productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling are FUNCTIONAL.
Examiners love planting 'stratification is a functional unit' as a false statement.
4. Standing crop vs standing state. Crop = biomass (living matter). State = nutrients. One letter of difference in your head, a full mark in the paper.
PRO-TIP: before writing any productivity answer, run the 'does it have a per?' check. If the quantity is not per area per time, it is a stock — not a productivity.
Mnemonics: 'GReN' — GPP, minus Respiration, gives NPP. And 'Crop is alive, State is in the soil'.

segments.text: Four traps live in this subtopic, and between them they account for almost every mark students drop here. Learn them as traps, not as facts.

Trap one: productivity versus standing crop. Productivity is per area per time. Standing crop is the biomass sitting there right now. Watch the wording of the question — rate of, means productivity; amount at a time, means standing crop. The examiner is telling you which one they want.

Trap two, and this is the big one. N P P equals G P P minus R of the producers. It is not G P P minus decomposition. And it is definitely not G P P plus R. Decomposers do not enter this equation at any point.

Trap three: the structure and function mix-up. Species composition and stratification are structural. Productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling are functional. Four functional, two structural.
And examiners plant this deliberately. The statement that stratification is a functional unit turns up again and again as a false option. Know it on sight.
Trap four: standing crop versus standing state. Crop is biomass, living matter. State is nutrients in the soil. One letter of difference in your head, and a full mark in the paper.

Now the pro-tip that dissolves half of these. Before you write any productivity answer, run the does it have a per check. If the quantity is not per area per time, it is a stock — a standing crop or a standing state — and you have probably picked the wrong term entirely.
<chuckle> And two mnemonics to carry in. G Re N, for the order of the productivity story: G P P, minus Respiration, gives N P P. And for the stock terms: crop is alive, state is in the soil.
इस subtopic में चार traps रहते हैं, और लगभग हर गिरा हुआ mark इन्हीं का किया-धरा है। इन्हें facts की तरह नहीं, traps की तरह याद कीजिए।

Trap एक: productivity बनाम standing crop। Productivity है per area per time। Standing crop है वह biomass जो अभी वहाँ खड़ी है। सवाल की wording देखिए — rate of, यानी productivity; amount at a time, यानी standing crop। Examiner ख़ुद बता रहा है कि उसे क्या चाहिए।
Trap दो, और यही सबसे बड़ा है। N P P बराबर G P P minus producers का R। यह G P P minus decomposition नहीं है। और G P P plus R तो बिलकुल नहीं। Decomposers इस equation में कहीं भी नहीं घुसते।

Trap तीन: structure और function की गड़बड़। Species composition और stratification structural हैं। Productivity, decomposition, energy flow और nutrient cycling functional हैं। चार functional, दो structural।
और examiners यह जान-बूझकर डालते हैं। यह statement कि stratification एक functional unit है, बार-बार false option की तरह आता है। इसे देखते ही पहचान लीजिए।
Trap चार: standing crop बनाम standing state। Crop यानी biomass, जीवित matter। State यानी मिट्टी में nutrients। दिमाग़ में एक अक्षर का फ़र्क़, और copy में पूरा एक mark।

अब वह pro-tip जो इनमें से आधे traps घोल देता है। कोई भी productivity का जवाब लिखने से पहले चलाइए — does it have a per? अगर quantity per area per time नहीं है, तो वह stock है — standing crop या standing state — और आपने शायद पूरा term ही ग़लत उठा लिया है।
<chuckle> और दो mnemonics साथ ले जाइए। G Re N, productivity की कहानी के order के लिए: G P P, minus Respiration, gives N P P। और stock terms के लिए: crop is alive, state is in the soil।

sections.title: Decomposition: the ecosystem's recycling plant

board_events.text: Decomposition = nature's recycling plant
Decomposers break down complex dead organic matter into simple inorganic substances — carbon dioxide, water and mineral nutrients — that producers can use all over again.

board_events.caption: Decomposition closes the loop: dead matter to decomposers to simple nutrients to producers

board_events.text: It is the step that CLOSES the loop every nutrient cycle depends on.
Scale: a single forest sheds tonnes of leaf litter every year — and every gram of it must be processed and returned.
Without decomposition every nutrient cycle would grind to a halt, and the soil would steadily lose its fertility.
The carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus in a fallen log or a dead animal are USELESS to a living plant until decomposers free them as simple inorganic ions.
This is also why decomposers (microbes) form the LARGEST population in a food chain — there is an enormous standing supply of dead matter for them to work on.

segments.text: Every leaf that falls and every animal that dies has to go somewhere. Otherwise the world would bury itself in its own dead matter, and lock all its nutrients away forever.

Decomposition is nature's recycling plant. It is the process by which decomposers break down complex dead organic matter into simple inorganic substances — carbon dioxide, water, and mineral nutrients — that producers can use all over again.
The board shows why it is called a loop. Dead matter goes in at one side, decomposers work on it, and simple nutrients come out and go straight back to the producers. Round and round, without end.
So this is the step that closes the loop every nutrient cycle depends on. Not a side-process, not a clean-up crew — the closing move, without which the cycle is not a cycle at all.

Consider the scale of the job. A single forest sheds tonnes of leaf litter every year, and every gram of it must be processed and returned, or the forest would smother in its own debris within a few seasons.
And here is the sentence that answers the why does this matter question. Without decomposition, every nutrient cycle would grind to a halt, and the soil would steadily lose its fertility.

Think about what that really means. The carbon, the nitrogen and the phosphorus locked inside a fallen log or a dead animal are completely useless to a living plant. Useless — until decomposers free them as simple inorganic ions. Decomposition is the only process that returns locked-up nutrients to circulation.

One more consequence worth carrying. This is exactly why decomposers, the microbes, are said to form the largest population in a food chain. There is an enormous standing supply of dead matter for them to work on — far more than the living biomass that herbivores ever eat.
जो भी पत्ता गिरता है और जो भी जानवर मरता है, उसे कहीं तो जाना ही है। वरना यह दुनिया अपने ही dead matter में दब जाती, और सारे nutrients हमेशा के लिए बंद हो जाते।

Decomposition nature का recycling plant है। यह वह process है जिसमें decomposers complex dead organic matter को तोड़कर simple inorganic substances बना देते हैं — carbon dioxide, पानी, और mineral nutrients — जिन्हें producers फिर से इस्तेमाल कर सकते हैं।

Board दिखा रहा है कि इसे loop क्यों कहते हैं। एक तरफ़ से dead matter जाता है, decomposers उस पर काम करते हैं, और दूसरी तरफ़ से simple nutrients निकलकर सीधे producers के पास लौट आते हैं। घूमता ही रहता है।
तो यही वह step है जो हर nutrient cycle का loop बंद करता है। कोई side-process नहीं, कोई सफ़ाई करने वाली team नहीं — यही closing move है, जिसके बिना cycle, cycle रह ही नहीं जाता।
काम का पैमाना भी सोचिए। एक अकेला forest हर साल टनों leaf litter गिराता है, और उसका हर gram process होकर लौटना चाहिए, वरना forest कुछ ही मौसमों में अपने ही कचरे में दब जाए।
और यह रही वह line जो यह matter क्यों करता है का जवाब देती है। Decomposition के बिना हर nutrient cycle रुक जाता, और मिट्टी लगातार अपनी fertility खोती चली जाती।

सोचिए इसका असली मतलब क्या है। गिरे हुए लट्ठे या मरे हुए जानवर में बंद carbon, nitrogen और phosphorus एक ज़िंदा पौधे के लिए बिलकुल बेकार हैं। बेकार — जब तक decomposers उन्हें simple inorganic ions की तरह आज़ाद न कर दें। Decomposition अकेला process है जो बंद पड़े nutrients को वापस circulation में लाता है।

एक और नतीजा साथ रखिए। यही वजह है कि decomposers यानी microbes को food chain की सबसे बड़ी population कहा जाता है। उनके काम के लिए dead matter का बहुत बड़ा standing supply मौजूद रहता है — उस living biomass से कहीं ज़्यादा जो herbivores कभी खाते हैं।

sections.title: Detritus, and the workers that eat from the outside

board_events.text: The raw material has a name: DETRITUS
Detritus — dead plant remains (fallen leaves, bark, flowers), dead animal bodies, and faecal matter.
ABOVE-GROUND detritus: leaf litter, dried plant parts, animal remains, droppings and excretions lying on the surface.
BELOW-GROUND detritus: dead roots, and the remains of underground animals.

<text x="505" y="318" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" fill="#dc2626" font-weight="bold">digest it internally</text>

board_events.caption: Detritus in two layers; and the saprotroph that digests outside and absorbs

board_events.text: The workers: decomposers — chiefly fungi and bacteria, also called SAPROTROPHS.
They secrete digestive enzymes ONTO the detritus, let the enzymes break it down externally, then absorb the dissolved products.
The whole of decomposition happens OUTSIDE their bodies. Because they feed by absorption from outside, they are also called OSMOTROPHS.
Useful contrast: animals INGEST food and digest it internally. An osmotroph never does.

segments.text: The raw material decomposers work on has a proper name, and the exam expects it: detritus.
Detritus is dead plant remains — fallen leaves, bark, flowers — plus dead animal bodies, and faecal matter. Anything that was alive and is now dead organic matter counts.

And it comes in two layers, which is a favourite one-mark question. Above-ground detritus is the leaf litter, the dried plant parts, the animal remains and their droppings and excretions lying on the surface.
Below-ground detritus is the dead roots, and the remains of underground animals. Same material, different address — and students routinely forget the second half exists.
Now look at the right-hand side of the board, because this is the strange part. The workers are the decomposers themselves — chiefly fungi and bacteria, also called saprotrophs.
<curious> And they have a genuinely unusual way of eating. Ask yourself: where does a fungus actually digest its food?
Here is the answer. It secretes digestive enzymes onto the detritus, lets the enzymes break it down externally, and then absorbs the dissolved products back in. Step one out, step two in.

So the whole of decomposition happens outside their bodies. And because they feed by absorption from the outside, they get a second name: osmotrophs. Saprotroph tells you what they eat; osmotroph tells you how.

Hold the contrast, because that is what the question is really testing. Animals ingest their food and digest it internally, inside a gut. An osmotroph never does. The enzymes go out; only the dissolved product comes in.
जिस raw material पर decomposers काम करते हैं, उसका एक proper नाम है, और exam वही माँगता है: detritus।
Detritus यानी dead plant remains — गिरे हुए पत्ते, छाल, फूल — साथ में dead animal bodies, और faecal matter। जो कुछ भी कभी ज़िंदा था और अब dead organic matter है, वह सब इसमें गिना जाता है।
और यह दो layers में आता है, जो favourite one-mark सवाल है। Above-ground detritus है leaf litter, सूखे plant parts, animal remains और उनकी droppings तथा excretions जो सतह पर पड़े हैं।
Below-ground detritus है dead roots, और ज़मीन के नीचे रहने वाले जानवरों के अवशेष। Material वही, पता अलग — और students अक्सर दूसरा आधा हिस्सा भूल ही जाते हैं।
अब board की दाईं तरफ़ देखिए, क्योंकि असली अजीब बात यही है। काम करने वाले हैं decomposers ख़ुद — मुख्यतः fungi और bacteria, जिन्हें saprotrophs भी कहते हैं।
<curious> और इनके खाने का तरीक़ा सचमुच अनोखा है। ख़ुद से पूछिए: एक fungus अपना खाना असल में पचाता कहाँ है?
जवाब यह है। वह digestive enzymes detritus पर छोड़ता है, enzymes को बाहर ही उसे तोड़ने देता है, और फिर घुले हुए products को वापस absorb कर लेता है। Step एक बाहर, step दो अंदर।

तो पूरी decomposition उनके शरीर के बाहर होती है। और चूँकि वे बाहर से absorption के ज़रिए खाते हैं, इसलिए उन्हें दूसरा नाम मिलता है: osmotrophs। Saprotroph बताता है वे क्या खाते हैं; osmotroph बताता है कैसे।

यह contrast पकड़ कर रखिए, क्योंकि सवाल असल में यही जाँचता है। जानवर खाना ingest करते हैं और उसे अंदर, gut में digest करते हैं। Osmotroph कभी ऐसा नहीं करता। Enzymes बाहर जाते हैं; अंदर सिर्फ़ घुला हुआ product आता है।

It falls to the ground. Some of it is eaten by insects and small animals — its nutrients and energy enter the food web.

board_events.caption: From falling leaf to fertile soil: the five stations of decomposition

board_events.text: Rain then leaches some soluble nutrients down into the soil.
Next, fungi and bacteria partially consume the leaf. It loses its shape and becomes LITTER.
Earthworms, soil mites, and more fungi and bacteria carry the breakdown further.
Finally the residue settles into organic-rich soil — from which a new tree can grow.
Decomposition is not a single event but a SET of processes — fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification, mineralisation — that largely run SIMULTANEOUSLY on the detritus.
The two end-products are always the same: HUMUS (a dark, resistant store of nutrients) and INORGANIC NUTRIENTS released back to the soil.

segments.text: Definitions are one thing. Watching the process actually happen is another. So follow a single green leaf, from the branch to the soil, and you will see the whole sequence without memorising a list.

It falls to the ground. Straight away, some of it is eaten by insects and small animals — and with that, its nutrients and its energy enter the food web. The leaf has begun feeding the ecosystem before it has decomposed at all.
The board lays the journey out as five stations. Read them left to right, and notice that the leaf is losing something different at each one.
Rain arrives next, and leaches some of the soluble nutrients down into the soil. Nothing has been chemically broken yet — this is water simply washing the easy fraction out and carrying it away.
Then fungi and bacteria partially consume the leaf. And here it stops being a leaf: it loses its shape, and what remains is called litter. The word litter is not casual — it marks a stage.
Earthworms, soil mites, and more fungi and bacteria carry the breakdown further, shredding and digesting what the first wave left behind.

And finally the residue settles into organic-rich soil, from which a new tree can grow. That journey — from falling leaf to fertile soil — is decomposition told as a story, and it is happening continuously across every forest floor right now.

So take the correction that follows. Decomposition is not a single event. It is a set of processes — fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and mineralisation — and they largely run simultaneously on the detritus, rather than in a neat one-after-another line.
But whatever the route, the exit is fixed. The two end-products are always the same: humus, a dark and resistant store of nutrients, and inorganic nutrients released back to the soil.
Definitions एक बात है। Process को होते हुए देखना दूसरी। तो एक हरे पत्ते के पीछे चलिए, टहनी से मिट्टी तक, और पूरी sequence बिना list रटे दिख जाएगी।

वह ज़मीन पर गिरता है। तुरंत ही उसका कुछ हिस्सा कीड़े और छोटे जानवर खा जाते हैं — और इसी के साथ उसके nutrients और energy food web में घुस जाते हैं। पत्ता decompose होने से पहले ही ecosystem को खिलाना शुरू कर देता है।
Board इस सफ़र को पाँच stations में रखता है। बाएँ से दाएँ पढ़िए, और ध्यान दीजिए कि हर station पर पत्ता कुछ अलग खो रहा है।
अब बारिश आती है, और कुछ soluble nutrients को मिट्टी में नीचे leach कर देती है। अभी तक chemically कुछ टूटा नहीं है — यह बस पानी है, जो आसान हिस्सा धोकर बहा ले जा रहा है।

फिर fungi और bacteria पत्ते को आंशिक रूप से खाते हैं। और यहीं वह पत्ता रहना बंद कर देता है: उसकी shape चली जाती है, और जो बचता है उसे litter कहते हैं। Litter शब्द यूँ ही नहीं है — यह एक stage का नाम है।
Earthworms, soil mites, और और भी fungi तथा bacteria breakdown को आगे बढ़ाते हैं, पहली लहर का छोड़ा हुआ हिस्सा चीरते और पचाते हुए।

और आख़िर में बचा हुआ हिस्सा organic-rich soil में बैठ जाता है, जिससे एक नया पेड़ उग सकता है। यह सफ़र — गिरते पत्ते से उपजाऊ मिट्टी तक — decomposition की कहानी है, और अभी इसी वक़्त हर forest floor पर लगातार चल रही है।

तो यह correction पकड़ लीजिए। Decomposition कोई एक event नहीं है। यह processes का एक set है — fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification और mineralisation — और ये ज़्यादातर detritus पर एक साथ चलते हैं, किसी सीधी एक-के-बाद-एक line में नहीं।
पर रास्ता चाहे जो हो, निकास तय है। दोनों end-products हमेशा वही रहते हैं: humus, यानी nutrients का एक गहरा और resistant भंडार, और inorganic nutrients जो मिट्टी में वापस छूट जाते हैं।

board_events.caption: Fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification, mineralisation — and the rate dials

board_events.text: 1. FRAGMENTATION — detritivores (earthworms, termites) chew and break detritus into small pieces. Why first: shredding hugely increases the surface area available to microbes and enzymes.
2. LEACHING — percolating water carries water-soluble inorganic nutrients down into the soil horizon, where they may precipitate as salts, temporarily unavailable to plants.
3. CATABOLISM — enzymes secreted by bacteria and fungi degrade the fragmented detritus, first into simpler organic material and then into simpler inorganic compounds. The actual chemical breakdown.
4. HUMIFICATION — part of the detritus is only partially broken down and accumulates as HUMUS: dark, amorphous, colloidal, resistant to microbes, slow to decompose, a reservoir of nutrients.
5. MINERALISATION — microbes slowly degrade the humus, releasing inorganic nutrients back into the soil for producers to reabsorb.
The numbering is a LOGICAL order, not a strict timetable. All five run simultaneously on different bits of detritus.
Why humus persists: its colloidal, chemically complex structure resists rapid microbial attack — improving soil texture and water-holding capacity along the way.

segments.text: There is no equation to derive here. The whole skill is getting the five steps in the right order, and knowing why each one happens. Get the reasons and the order comes free.
The board holds all five at once, so keep your eye on it as we walk across. Detritus enters on the left; inorganic nutrients leave on the right.

Step one, fragmentation. Detritivores such as earthworms, and termites, chew and break the detritus into small pieces. And why does this have to come first? Because shredding hugely increases the surface area available to microbes and enzymes. A whole leaf rots far more slowly than the same leaf torn into a hundred fragments.

Step two, leaching. Percolating water carries the water-soluble inorganic nutrients down into the soil horizon, where they may precipitate as salts that are temporarily unavailable to plants. Water is simply the transport medium here, moving the soluble fraction out of the litter layer and into the soil profile.

Step three, catabolism. Enzymes secreted by bacteria and fungi chemically degrade the fragmented detritus — first into simpler organic material, then into simpler inorganic compounds. This is the actual chemical breakdown, the heart of decomposition, where complex molecules are dismantled bond by bond.

Step four, humification. Part of the detritus is only partially broken down, and it accumulates as humus: dark, amorphous, colloidal, resistant to microbes, slow to decompose, and a reservoir of nutrients. Humification builds a store.

Step five, mineralisation. Microbes slowly degrade that humus, releasing inorganic nutrients back into the soil for producers to reabsorb. Why last? Because it unlocks what the resistant humus was holding, completing the recycling and feeding the nutrient cycles.
Now the caveat that examiners hide in true-or-false questions. The numbering is a logical order, not a strict timetable. All five run simultaneously, on different bits of detritus, all the time.

One last thing about humus, because it gets asked directly. Why does it persist? Its colloidal, chemically complex structure resists rapid microbial attack, so it lingers in the soil for a long time — improving soil texture and water-holding capacity along the way.
यहाँ कोई equation derive नहीं करनी। पूरी skill यही है कि पाँचों steps सही order में आएँ, और हर step की वजह पता हो। वजहें आ गईं तो order मुफ़्त में आ जाएगा।
Board पर पाँचों एक साथ हैं, तो नज़र वहीं रखिए जब हम इन पर चलें। बाईं तरफ़ detritus घुसता है; दाईं तरफ़ inorganic nutrients निकलते हैं।

Step एक, fragmentation। Detritivores जैसे earthworms, और termites, detritus को चबाकर छोटे टुकड़ों में तोड़ते हैं। और यह सबसे पहले क्यों आना चाहिए? क्योंकि टुकड़े करने से microbes और enzymes के लिए surface area ज़बरदस्त बढ़ जाता है। एक पूरा पत्ता उसी पत्ते के सौ टुकड़ों के मुक़ाबले कहीं धीमे सड़ता है।

Step दो, leaching। रिसता हुआ पानी water-soluble inorganic nutrients को soil horizon में नीचे ले जाता है, जहाँ वे salts की तरह precipitate हो सकते हैं और पौधों के लिए फ़िलहाल unavailable हो जाते हैं। पानी यहाँ बस transport medium है, जो soluble हिस्से को litter layer से निकालकर soil profile में पहुँचा देता है।

Step तीन, catabolism। Bacteria और fungi के छोड़े हुए enzymes टुकड़ों वाले detritus को chemically तोड़ते हैं — पहले simpler organic material में, फिर simpler inorganic compounds में। यही असली chemical breakdown है, decomposition का दिल, जहाँ complex molecules एक-एक bond करके खोले जाते हैं।

Step चार, humification। Detritus का कुछ हिस्सा सिर्फ़ आंशिक रूप से टूटता है, और humus की तरह जमा हो जाता है: गहरा, amorphous, colloidal, microbes के लिए resistant, बहुत धीरे decompose होने वाला, और nutrients का reservoir। Humification एक भंडार बनाती है।

Step पाँच, mineralisation। Microbes उसी humus को धीरे-धीरे तोड़ते हैं, और inorganic nutrients मिट्टी में वापस छोड़ते हैं, ताकि producers उन्हें दोबारा ले सकें। सबसे आख़िर में क्यों? क्योंकि यही उस resistant humus की पकड़ खोलता है, recycling पूरी करता है और nutrient cycles को खिलाता है।
अब वह caveat जो examiners true-or-false में छिपाते हैं। यह numbering एक logical order है, कोई सख़्त timetable नहीं। पाँचों एक साथ चलते हैं, detritus के अलग-अलग टुकड़ों पर, हर वक़्त।

Humus के बारे में आख़िरी बात, क्योंकि यह सीधे पूछी जाती है। यह टिकता क्यों है? इसकी colloidal और chemically complex बनावट तेज़ microbial attack को रोक देती है, इसलिए यह मिट्टी में लंबे समय तक बना रहता है — और साथ-साथ soil texture और water-holding capacity भी सुधारता है।

sections.title: Framework B: the four dials that set the rate

board_events.caption: The four controls on decomposition rate: chemistry, climate, aeration and soil pH

board_events.text: Chemical nature of detritus: rich in cellulose, lignin, tannin or resin means SLOW. Rich in protein, nucleic acids, nitrogen or water-soluble sugars means FAST.
Climate: higher temperature and soil moisture means faster. Warm plus moist is ideal.
Aeration / oxygen: aerobic means faster; anaerobiosis means slower. Decomposition NEEDS oxygen.
This is why dead plant matter accumulates rather than rotting away in waterlogged bogs and marshes.
Soil pH: influences which microbes thrive — broadly, acidic soils decompose slowly, more alkaline soils faster.
Putting it together: fastest in a tropical rainforest (warm, humid, well-aerated soil); slowest in cold or arid regions like the Antarctic or a desert.
Most decomposition happens in the UPPER layer of the soil, where detritus is most abundant and oxygen most available.

segments.text: Decomposition is not one speed everywhere. It speeds up and slows down, and it does so on exactly four dials. Learn the dials and you can predict any site the exam invents.
The board sets them out as four rows — red on the left for slow, green on the right for fast. Every question about rate is asking you to read one of these rows.

Dial one, the chemical nature of the detritus. Detritus rich in cellulose, lignin, tannin or resin decomposes slowly. Detritus rich in protein, nucleic acids, nitrogen or water-soluble sugars decomposes fast.
Dial two, climate. Higher temperature and higher soil moisture mean faster decomposition. Warm plus moist is the ideal combination, and both halves matter — warm and dry will not do it.
Dial three, aeration. Aerobic conditions mean faster; anaerobiosis means slower. Decomposition is an oxygen-requiring process — the microbes need oxygen, full stop.

And that dial has a famous consequence, so read the red note. In waterlogged, airless conditions the microbes are throttled, so dead plant matter accumulates rather than rotting away. That is exactly why bogs and marshes pile up organic matter instead of clearing it.
Dial four, soil pH. It influences which microbes thrive — and broadly, acidic soils decompose slowly, while more alkaline soils decompose faster.

Now put all four together and a prediction falls out. Decomposition is fastest in a tropical rainforest: warm, humid, well-aerated soil, all three dials turned up. And it is slowest in cold or arid regions — the Antarctic, or a desert.

It is also worth knowing why chemistry matters so much. Lignin, chitin, tannin and resin are large, complex, chemically stable molecules that few microbial enzymes can attack quickly, so woody twigs, bark and insect cuticle linger for a long time. Nitrogen-rich tissue and soluble sugars are what microbes prefer. A gardener sees it directly — green kitchen scraps rot in weeks, while a dry woody branch can sit in the compost heap for a year.
Decomposition की रफ़्तार हर जगह एक जैसी नहीं होती। यह तेज़ भी होती है और धीमी भी, और ठीक चार dials पर होती है। Dials समझ लीजिए, तो exam चाहे जो site गढ़े, आप भविष्यवाणी कर लेंगे।
Board इन्हें चार rows में रखता है — बाईं तरफ़ लाल यानी slow, दाईं तरफ़ हरा यानी fast। Rate का हर सवाल आपसे इन्हीं में से कोई एक row पढ़वाना चाहता है।
Dial एक, detritus की chemical nature। Cellulose, lignin, tannin या resin से भरा detritus धीरे decompose होता है। Protein, nucleic acids, nitrogen या water-soluble sugars से भरा detritus तेज़।
Dial दो, climate। ज़्यादा temperature और ज़्यादा soil moisture मतलब तेज़ decomposition। Warm plus moist ideal combination है, और दोनों हिस्से ज़रूरी हैं — सिर्फ़ गरम और सूखा काम नहीं आएगा।
Dial तीन, aeration। Aerobic conditions मतलब तेज़; anaerobiosis मतलब धीमा। Decomposition एक oxygen-requiring process है — microbes को oxygen चाहिए, बस।

और इस dial का एक मशहूर नतीजा है, तो लाल note पढ़िए। पानी भरे, हवा-रहित हालात में microbes घुट जाते हैं, इसलिए dead plant matter सड़ने के बजाय जमा होता चला जाता है। यही वजह है कि bogs और marshes organic matter साफ़ करने के बजाय उसका ढेर लगा लेते हैं।
Dial चार, soil pH। यह तय करता है कि कौन से microbes पनपेंगे — और मोटे तौर पर, acidic soils धीरे decompose करती हैं, जबकि ज़्यादा alkaline soils तेज़।

अब चारों को जोड़िए और भविष्यवाणी अपने आप निकल आती है। Decomposition सबसे तेज़ tropical rainforest में होती है: warm, humid, well-aerated soil — तीनों dials ऊपर। और सबसे धीमी ठंडे या शुष्क इलाक़ों में — Antarctic, या रेगिस्तान।

यह भी जानना ज़रूरी है कि chemistry इतनी क्यों मायने रखती है। Lignin, chitin, tannin और resin बड़े, complex, chemically stable molecules हैं जिन पर बहुत कम microbial enzymes जल्दी हमला कर पाते हैं, इसलिए लकड़ी की टहनियाँ, छाल और insect cuticle बहुत देर तक पड़े रहते हैं। Nitrogen वाले tissue और घुलनशील शक्कर microbes की पसंद हैं। कोई भी माली यह सीधे देख लेता है — हरे kitchen scraps हफ़्तों में सड़ जाते हैं, जबकि सूखी लकड़ी की डाल compost heap में साल भर पड़ी रह सकती है।

board_events.text: Whatever the detritus, decomposition yields TWO things: humus (the dark, resistant nutrient store) and inorganic nutrients — carbon dioxide, water and minerals released to the soil.
Most of this activity is concentrated in the UPPER layer of the soil — that is where detritus accumulates, and where oxygen and microbes are most available.
The deeper you go, the less decomposition occurs.
The inorganic nutrients freed here are precisely what feeds back into the nutrient cycles — linking this subtopic directly to the carbon and phosphorus cycles.
One more connection: the dead matter decomposers process is also the starting point of the DETRITUS FOOD CHAIN — detritus, then detritivores, then their predators.

In a terrestrial ecosystem a much larger fraction of energy flows through this detritus pathway than through the grazing food chain. The same dead leaf is food for a detritivore AND a source of recycled minerals.

segments.text: Two questions remain about decomposition, and both get asked directly. What comes out of it, and where does it actually happen? Framework C settles both.
The board answers the first question on the right and the second on the left. Take the products first.

Whatever the detritus was, decomposition yields exactly two things. Humus — the dark, resistant nutrient store. And inorganic nutrients — carbon dioxide, water and minerals, released to the soil. Two products, every time, no exceptions.

Now the place. Most of this activity is concentrated in the upper layer of the soil. And there is no mystery to it: that is simply where detritus accumulates, and where oxygen and microbes are most available.
Which gives you the gradient on the left of the board. The deeper you go, the less decomposition occurs. Litter layer, busy. Upper soil, busiest. Below that, quieter and quieter.

And read the red note, because it is the bridge to the rest of the chapter. The inorganic nutrients freed here are precisely what feeds back into the nutrient cycles — which links this subtopic directly to the carbon and the phosphorus cycles you will meet later.

There is one more connection worth holding in view, and it is the one students miss. The dead matter that decomposers process is also the starting point of the detritus food chain: detritus, then detritivores, then their predators.

And in a terrestrial ecosystem, a much larger fraction of energy actually flows through this detritus pathway than through the grazing food chain. Which is another way of saying decomposition is not a side-process. The same dead leaf is simultaneously food for a detritivore, which is energy, and a source of recycled minerals, which is nutrients. Decomposition sits at the junction of both.
Decomposition के बारे में दो सवाल बाक़ी हैं, और दोनों सीधे पूछे जाते हैं। इससे निकलता क्या है, और यह होती असल में कहाँ है? Framework C दोनों निपटा देता है।
Board पहला सवाल दाईं तरफ़ और दूसरा बाईं तरफ़ हल करता है। पहले products लीजिए।

Detritus चाहे जो रहा हो, decomposition से ठीक दो चीज़ें निकलती हैं। Humus — गहरा, resistant nutrient भंडार। और inorganic nutrients — carbon dioxide, पानी और minerals, जो मिट्टी में छूट जाते हैं। दो products, हर बार, बिना अपवाद।
अब जगह। यह सारी गतिविधि ज़्यादातर मिट्टी की upper layer में केंद्रित रहती है। और इसमें कोई रहस्य नहीं: बस वहीं detritus जमा होता है, और वहीं oxygen तथा microbes सबसे ज़्यादा उपलब्ध हैं।
इसी से board की बाईं तरफ़ वाला gradient बनता है। जितना गहरा जाइए, उतनी कम decomposition होती है। Litter layer में हलचल। Upper soil में सबसे ज़्यादा। उसके नीचे, धीरे-धीरे शांत।

और लाल note पढ़िए, क्योंकि यही बाक़ी chapter तक का पुल है। यहाँ आज़ाद हुए inorganic nutrients ही वे हैं जो nutrient cycles को वापस खिलाते हैं — जो इस subtopic को सीधे carbon और phosphorus cycles से जोड़ देता है, जो आपको आगे मिलेंगे।

एक और connection नज़र में रखने लायक़ है, और यही students से छूटता है। जिस dead matter पर decomposers काम करते हैं, वही detritus food chain की शुरुआत भी है: detritus, फिर detritivores, फिर उनके predators।

और terrestrial ecosystem में energy का कहीं बड़ा हिस्सा असल में इसी detritus रास्ते से बहता है, न कि grazing food chain से। यानी दूसरे शब्दों में, decomposition कोई side-process नहीं है। वही एक मरा हुआ पत्ता एक साथ detritivore का खाना है, जो energy है, और recycled minerals का स्रोत भी, जो nutrients है। Decomposition दोनों के जोड़ पर बैठी है।

board_events.caption: Humification builds the humus store; mineralisation empties it

board_events.text: Sequence: fragmentation, then leaching, then catabolism, then humification, then mineralisation.
Humification is the ACCUMULATION of humus — a dark, resistant store of nutrients. Mineralisation is the later BREAKDOWN of that humus by microbes, to release inorganic nutrients.
One stores, the other releases. Opposite directions.
Example 2 — CUET / Speed Trap
An earthworm shredding fallen leaves, and a fungus releasing minerals from humus — which is the detritivore and which the decomposer? Why are both grouped under 'the decomposition community'?

Earthworm physically breaks detritus into pieces, so it is a DETRITIVORE (a fragmenter). Fungus chemically frees inorganic nutrients, so it is a DECOMPOSER / mineraliser. They work as a relay on the same dead matter: one prepares the surface area, the other completes the chemistry.
Trap cue: 'breaks into pieces' means detritivore. 'Releases nutrients / secretes enzymes' means decomposer.

segments.text: Example one, from the C B S E boards. Two demands are packed into one question here, and you must answer both explicitly — half the marks walk away if you answer only the first.
Name, in correct sequence, the five steps of decomposition, and distinguish humification from mineralisation. Sequence first, distinction second. Do them in that order on the page.
The board is already doing the second half for you. Look at the two arrows: one points into the humus box, the other points out of it. That is the entire distinction in a single picture.

Take the sequence first, and write it as a chain, not as a scattered list. Fragmentation. Then leaching. Then catabolism. Then humification. Then mineralisation. Five steps, fragmentation first, mineralisation last.

Now the distinction, half by half. Humification is the accumulation of humus — a dark, resistant store of nutrients; it builds the store. Mineralisation is the later breakdown of that humus by microbes, releasing inorganic nutrients into the soil; it empties the store.
So say it in one line and the examiner cannot mark you down: one stores, the other releases. Opposite directions, on the very same material.
Example two, a C U E T speed trap — and the whole thing turns on reading a single verb.
An earthworm is shredding fallen leaves. A fungus is releasing minerals from humus. Which is the detritivore and which the decomposer, and why are both grouped under the decomposition community?

Read the verb and the answer arrives before the sentence ends. The earthworm physically breaks detritus into pieces, so it is a detritivore, a fragmenter. The fungus chemically frees inorganic nutrients, so it is a decomposer, a mineraliser. They are grouped together because they work as a relay on the same dead matter: the detritivore prepares the material, giving it more surface area, and the decomposer completes the chemical breakdown.

One more layer, because it usually carries the second mark. The fungus, being a saprotroph, digests externally and absorbs — an osmotroph — whereas the earthworm ingests and processes internally. And bank the trap cue: breaks into pieces means detritivore; releases nutrients, or secretes enzymes, means decomposer.
Example एक, C B S E boards से। यहाँ एक ही सवाल में दो माँगें ठूँसी हुई हैं, और दोनों साफ़-साफ़ लिखनी हैं — सिर्फ़ पहली का जवाब दिया तो आधे marks यूँ ही चले जाएँगे।
Decomposition के पाँच steps सही sequence में बताइए, और humification को mineralisation से अलग कीजिए। पहले sequence, फिर distinction। copy पर भी इसी order में लिखिए।
Board दूसरा आधा हिस्सा पहले ही आपके लिए कर रहा है। दोनों arrows देखिए: एक humus के डिब्बे के अंदर जा रहा है, दूसरा उसमें से बाहर। पूरा फ़र्क़ बस इसी एक तस्वीर में है।

पहले sequence लीजिए, और इसे एक chain की तरह लिखिए, बिखरी हुई list की तरह नहीं। Fragmentation. फिर leaching. फिर catabolism. फिर humification. फिर mineralisation. पाँच steps, fragmentation पहला, mineralisation आख़िरी।

अब distinction, आधा-आधा करके। Humification है humus का accumulation — nutrients का एक गहरा, resistant भंडार; यह भंडार बनाती है। Mineralisation है उसी humus का बाद में microbes द्वारा breakdown, जिससे inorganic nutrients मिट्टी में छूटते हैं; यह भंडार ख़ाली करती है।
तो एक line में कह दीजिए और examiner काट ही नहीं सकता: एक stores करती है, दूसरी releases करती है। ठीक उसी material पर, उल्टी दिशाएँ।
Example दो, एक C U E T speed trap — और पूरा मामला बस एक verb पढ़ने पर टिका है।
एक earthworm गिरे हुए पत्ते चीर रहा है। एक fungus humus से minerals छोड़ रहा है। कौन detritivore है और कौन decomposer, और दोनों को decomposition community में क्यों रखा जाता है?

Verb पढ़िए और जवाब वाक्य ख़त्म होने से पहले आ जाता है। Earthworm detritus को physically टुकड़ों में तोड़ता है, तो वह detritivore है, एक fragmenter। Fungus chemically inorganic nutrients आज़ाद करता है, तो वह decomposer है, एक mineraliser। दोनों साथ रखे जाते हैं क्योंकि वे एक ही dead matter पर relay की तरह काम करते हैं: detritivore material तैयार करता है और उसे ज़्यादा surface area देता है, और decomposer chemical breakdown पूरा करता है।

एक परत और, क्योंकि दूसरा mark अक्सर यही देता है। Fungus, saprotroph होने के नाते, बाहर digest करके absorb करता है — यानी osmotroph — जबकि earthworm ingest करके अंदर process करता है। और trap cue याद रखिए: टुकड़ों में तोड़ना मतलब detritivore; nutrients छोड़ना या enzymes secrete करना मतलब decomposer।
